title: Worldly right view
hook: that giving bears fruit, that deeds matter, that there are good teachers (MN 117)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kusala, and your line, a root being watered. Did you catch which root a moment was growing from, and water a different one? Day three hundred fifty-six.

Six in the morning, a village road, and a grandmother who has never read a sutta is already waiting with a pot of rice for the monks' bowls. She does this every day. She's honest at the market. She tells her grandchildren that what you do comes back to you, that your parents deserve respect, that there are good people in the world worth listening to. Does she have right view? Or is right view only for scholars who can recite the twelve links? The Buddha's answer, in a sutta about the path's factors, is that there are two kinds of right view. And the grandmother has the first one. Today, worldly right view.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER WHO NEVER READ A SUTTA.` → `RICE, HONESTY, RESPECT.` → `TWO KINDS OF RIGHT VIEW.`

segments.voice: The sutta is number one hundred seventeen in the Middle-Length Discourses, the Great Forty. In it the Buddha says right view is twofold. There's right view that is still bound up with the world, sharing in merit and ripening in good results. And there's right view that is noble, beyond the world: the wisdom of someone who has entered the path for real. Then he spells out the worldly kind, as a list of things a person holds to be so. There is what is given: giving bears fruit. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is this world and the other world. There is mother and father, which the commentaries read as: they matter, and are owed gratitude. There are beings reborn spontaneously. And there are good, well-practiced teachers in the world who have seen these things for themselves and make them known. Notice what's on that list. Not complicated philosophy. Basic confidence that actions have consequences, that generosity isn't wasted, that parents and teachers count. In Pali, the action is kamma, karma in Sanskrit, and its result is vipaka, the ripening. The Buddha doesn't call worldly right view second-rate; teachers often describe it as the ground the noble kind grows from. And again and again in the same sutta he says right view comes first, because it lets you tell wrong view as wrong and right view as right. So the grandmother at the roadside with her rice pot isn't doing something less than the scholar. She's standing on the first floor of the same house. Modern Buddhists hold different views about rebirth and other worlds, and teachers address that in different ways. The list's center holds across them: deeds matter.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF RIGHT VIEW.` · `GIVING BEARS FRUIT.` · `KAMMA AND ITS RIPENING.` · `THE GROUND THE NOBLE KIND GROWS FROM.` · then, large: `DEEDS MATTER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice one fruit of a deed. Sit and breathe. Think of one kind thing someone did for you long ago, a teacher who stayed late, a stranger who helped. Notice whether it still lives in you. That's a fruit. Then think of one small thing you did for someone else, and imagine it ripening in them, quietly, somewhere you'll never see. Let both rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Vipaka, the ripening of an action's result. Worldly right view: giving bears fruit, deeds have results, parents matter, and good teachers exist, the ground of the path.
Your line: deeds matter. Today, do one small thing as if it will ripen somewhere: hold a door, send a thank-you, clean up a mess you didn't make. Day three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In Theravada lay practice, right view is often lived as confidence in kamma: giving to monks and the needy, honoring parents and teachers, and trusting that good actions bear good fruit.

match.prompt: match each piece of worldly right view.
pairs: the wisdom of one on the path

myth: in MN 117 the Buddha says right view is twofold
worldly right view, sharing in merit, and noble right view, beyond the world.
worldly right view is dismissed as useless
the sutta counts it as right view; teachers describe it as the ground of the noble kind.

it's on the list, along with giving, deeds and good teachers.

fork.setup: a grandmother gives rice to monks every morning, is honest at market, and honors her parents. she's never read a sutta. by MN 117, does she have right view?
options: only if she can recite the twelve links.
fork.reveal: MN 117 counts confidence that giving bears fruit and deeds matter as right view: the worldly kind, ground of the noble kind.

original.note: Pali kamma, Sanskrit karma: intentional action; its result is called vipāka, ripening.

trapdoor: what you thought: right view is only for advanced meditators.
what it means: there's worldly right view too: confidence that deeds matter, the ground of the deeper kind.

what a scholar hears: MN 117 distinguishes sāsava sammā diṭṭhi, with taints and sharing in merit, from ariya anāsava lokuttara sammā diṭṭhi, noble and supramundane, the wisdom faculty of one on the path.
recall: to be realized, seen for yourself

notes: MN 117 paraphrased: confirm the list (there is what is given, offered, sacrificed; fruit of good and bad deeds; this world and the other world; mother and father; spontaneously reborn beings; good recluses and brahmins who declare these things) and the two kinds of right view.
Gloss 'there is mother and father' as 'they matter and are owed gratitude' is the usual commentarial reading; confirm.
The sentence that 'right view goes first' paraphrases MN 117's repeated 'right view comes first' (pubbaṅgamā); confirm.
The note that modern Buddhists differ on rebirth is stated neutrally; Keeper may adjust.

Editor review: hook no longer opens with 'Picture' and no longer tells the listener what they think; the parents gloss is now attributed to the commentaries; 'the ground the noble kind grows from' is attributed to teachers, not to the sutta; corrected 'in a later passage... right view goes first' to MN 117's repeated 'right view comes first' (it opens every section, not one later passage); practice and howItsDone softened ('feel how', 'for many lay Buddhists').
